Any two of:

  • electrons are excited/promoted to higher energy levels (by heat or electricity);
  • they then fall back to lower energy levels;
  • emitting energy as light of a specific frequency as they do so.

Because energy levels are discrete, only certain frequencies are emitted → a line spectrum.

Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate (equal-energy) p orbitals singly before pairing, because two electrons in the same orbital repel each other.

Ti: 1s22s22p63s23p63d24s2 (or …4s23d2, or [Ar]3d24s2).

(i) The 2nd electron is removed from a positive ion, Be+, whereas the 1st is removed from a neutral atom; the electron is held more strongly by the greater effective attraction, so IE2 > IE1.

(ii) In Al the electron is removed from a 3p sublevel, which is higher in energy (and slightly shielded by 3s) than the 3s electron removed from Mg, so less energy is needed.

(iii) In B the electron comes from 2p, in Al from 3p; the Al electron is further from the nucleus (more shielding), so it is easier to remove.

The spectrum is a series of discrete coloured lines (not continuous) that get closer together (converge) at higher frequency/energy (shorter wavelength).

Each line is produced when an excited electron falls from a higher to a lower energy level; the energy levels are fixed (quantized), so each transition emits a photon of one particular energy, ΔE = hν. Convergence occurs because the energy levels get closer together at higher energy.

(i) The first three IEs increase steadily (each electron removed from an increasingly positive ion), then there is a large jump from the 3rd to the 4th IE because the 4th electron comes from a full inner shell (2p) closer to the nucleus.

(ii) B: 1s²2s²2p¹; Al: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹; Mg: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s².

Al < B: Al's outer electron is in a higher energy level (n = 3), further from the nucleus and more shielded, so easier to remove.

Al < Mg: Al's electron is removed from a 3p sublevel, which is higher in energy than Mg's 3s, so it is easier to remove (despite Al's higher nuclear charge).

Sketch: a series of discrete lines that get closer together (converge) towards the high-energy end (high frequency/short wavelength), labelled.

Explanation: electrons are excited to higher energy levels in the discharge; when they fall back to lower levels they emit photons whose energy equals the (fixed) difference between levels, so only certain frequencies appear.

A continuous spectrum contains all wavelengths/frequencies (colours) in a range; a line spectrum contains only certain discrete wavelengths, seen as sharp lines.
Draw four lines that get closer together towards the high-energy end (converging). Why: energy levels in the atom get closer together as n increases.

Each line corresponds to an electron falling between two specific energy levels, emitting a photon of fixed energy (ΔE = hf). Only discrete lines appear, so electrons can only have certain (quantised) energies — i.e. energy levels exist.

(i) 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (full configuration; not [Ne]3s23p6 or 2,8,8).

(ii) One positive ion, e.g. K+ / Ca2+, and one negative ion, e.g. Cl− / S2− / P3− (all have 18 electrons).

Any three species with 10 electrons, e.g. Ne, Na+, Al3+, F−, O2−, N3−. [2] for three, [1] for two.

(i) Mg’s outer electron is in the 3rd shell (3s), further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons than F’s 2p electron, so it is less strongly attracted.

(ii) Mg2+(g) → Mg3+(g) + e−. Now the electron is removed from the 2p level (Mg2+ has the Ne configuration), the same level as in F, but Mg has more protons (12 vs 9), so a much greater attraction.

(i) Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion. The nuclear charge stays the same but there are fewer electrons (less repulsion), so the remaining electrons are held more tightly.

(ii) For Na there are big jumps after the 1st and after the 9th electron (pattern 1 : 8 : 2).

  • The 1st electron (3s) is far from the nucleus, so it is easily removed.
  • The next 8 (n = 2) are much closer, so their IE is much higher.
  • The last 2 (n = 1) are closest, so they have the highest IE.
The large jumps show changes of main energy level, so there are three levels.

  • …in the gaseous state.

• Al ([Ne]3s23p1) loses an electron from a 3p sub-level; Mg ([Ne]3s2) loses one from 3s.
  • The 3p sub-level is higher in energy (further from the nucleus and more shielded by the 3s electrons), so less energy is needed.

• The third electron is removed from an already positive ion (Mg2+), so there is more attraction to it.
  • It comes from the second energy level (n = 2), a full inner shell much closer to the nucleus and less shielded. The first electron comes from n = 3.

• The spectrum is a series of discrete lines (a line spectrum), not continuous.
  • Each line arises from an electron falling from a higher to a lower energy level, emitting a photon of energy equal to the gap (transitions to n = 1 give the UV series, to n = 2 the visible series, to n = 3 the IR series).
  • The lines converge (get closer together) at higher frequency / energy / shorter wavelength, because the energy levels get closer together.

• Vertical axis labelled energy; levels labelled n = 1, 2, 3 …
  • At least four levels, getting closer together (converging) towards n = ∞.
  • UV (Lyman) series: arrows from higher levels down to n = 1 (at least two lines).
  • Visible (Balmer) series: arrows from higher levels down to n = 2 (at least two lines).

Arrows must point downwards (emission).

Draw an arrow upwards from n = 1 to n = ∞. Ionization means removing the electron completely from the atom – from the ground state (n = 1) to beyond the influence of the nucleus (n = ∞); the length of this arrow is the first IE.

Na: 1s22s22p63s1 (full form, not [Ne]3s1). Any three:

  • 1st IE lowest: a single electron in n = 3, furthest from the nucleus and well shielded.
  • Large jump from 1st to 2nd IE: the 2nd electron comes from n = 2, closer to the nucleus.
  • Electrons 2–9 show a gradual increase: all from the same level (n = 2).
  • Large jump from 9th to 10th IE: electrons 10 and 11 come from n = 1, closest to the nucleus and least shielded (small increase from 10th to 11th).

(i) Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, which is higher in energy (further from the nucleus) and shielded by the 3s electrons, than Mg's 3s electron – so it is easier to remove.

(ii) In S (3p4) one 3p orbital holds a pair of electrons; repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove than from P (3p3, all unpaired).

Cu: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s1 (a full 3d sublevel is more stable, so it is not 3d94s2).

Cu+: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10; the 4s electron is lost first.

A full configuration is asked for, so the [Ar] shorthand is penalized.

(i) The energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from one mole of gaseous atoms. Equation: Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e− (gaseous state symbols are required).

(ii) Each electron after the first is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so the electrostatic attraction for the remaining electrons is greater.

(iii) The 10th electron comes from the second energy level (n = 2), but the 11th comes from the first level (n = 1). That electron is closer to the nucleus and is not shielded by inner electrons, so it feels a much greater effective nuclear charge. The result is the big jump between the 10th and 11th ionization energies.
Co2+: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d7 ([Ar]3d7). The 4s electrons are lost first, so it is not 3d54s2.

(i) [Ar] is shorthand for the electron configuration of argon, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (the noble-gas core).

(ii) x = 1, y = 5. Cr is [Ar]4s13d5: a half-filled d sublevel is more stable.

(iii) One arrow in the 4s box and one arrow in each of the five 3d boxes, all with parallel spins (Hund's rule): six unpaired electrons.

Why: transition metals lose 4s electrons first (Co is [Ar]3d74s2; remove 2 × 4s and 1 × 3d). The full configuration is required, not [Ar]3d6.

(i) Ti: 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d2; the first electron is removed from the 4s sub-level.

(ii) The 4th electron comes from 3d but the 5th from 3p – a lower energy level, closer to the nucleus. Likewise the 10th is from 3p and the 11th from 3s, a sub-level that penetrates closer to the nucleus. Electrons in levels closer to the nucleus experience greater effective nuclear charge / less shielding so are held more strongly – large jump. [3 max]

(iii) +2, +3, +4.

(iv) Colour requires a partially filled d sub-level: in a complex the d orbitals are split into two sets of different energies; an electron absorbs visible light to jump to the higher set. Ni2+ (3d8) has an incomplete 3d sub-level, but Sc3+ (3d0) has no d electrons, so no d–d transition and it is colourless. Ni2+ absorbs red light, so the complementary colour green is seen.

(ii) [3 max] Electrons in excited atoms fall from higher to lower energy levels (to n = 2 for the visible series); each transition emits light of a specific frequency because ΔE = hf; energy levels are discrete so only certain lines appear; the levels get closer together at higher energy, so lines converge.

(ii) n = 4 has n2 = 16 orbitals (1 s + 3 p + 5 d + 7 f).

The minimum energy needed to remove one electron (the outermost) from a gaseous atom (per mole: X(g) → X+(g) + e−).

(i) Any two: the second electron is removed from the same (3s) sublevel; it is removed from a positive ion, so it is held more strongly/closer to the nucleus; there is less electron–electron repulsion in Mg+.

(ii) Any two: the third electron comes from a lower energy level (2p, a full stable shell); it is much closer to the nucleus; it experiences less shielding/greater effective nuclear charge.

(i) As electrons are removed, the remaining electrons experience less repulsion and are pulled closer by the same nuclear charge (ion gets smaller), so each is harder to remove.

(ii) The 10th electron is in the second shell (n = 2); the 11th is removed from the first shell (n = 1), much closer to the nucleus and with no shielding, so far more energy is needed.

The full configuration is required; [Ar] shorthand is not accepted.

(i) First: 4s; second: 4s; third: 3d; fourth: 3d (4s is lost first in ions).

(ii) Electrons are removed from an increasingly positive ion in the same sublevel: less electron–electron repulsion, so the remaining electrons are held more tightly.

(iii) Electron 5 is the last 3d (valence) electron; electron 6 comes from the 3p sublevel of a complete inner shell, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded (higher effective nuclear charge), so far more energy is needed.

(ii) The ionization energy of hydrogen (E = hf at the convergence limit).

(i) Ti2+: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2 (both 4s electrons are lost first).

(ii) V has a smaller ionic/atomic radius (and one more valence electron to delocalize), so its metallic bonding is stronger.

(iii) A steady, gradual increase for IE1–IE5 (4s23d3), then a sharp jump at the 6th (removed from the inner 3p). A log plot is acceptable.

(iv) Ti atoms/ions are a different size from Al atoms and distort the regular lattice, which stops the layers sliding over each other easily.

Electrons occupy discrete (quantized) energy levels/shells around the nucleus. The energy levels converge (get closer together) at higher energy, i.e. further from the nucleus. Each line in the spectrum corresponds to an electron falling between two levels.

Any two of: the 4th electron is removed from an inner (lower) shell (a full, stable shell – the element is Al, group 13); it is closer to the nucleus; it experiences less shielding (a higher effective nuclear charge), so it is held much more tightly.

• It is a line spectrum: a series of discrete lines at only certain frequencies/wavelengths (not continuous).
• The lines converge (get closer together) at higher frequency/energy, i.e. shorter wavelength.

Each line is produced when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, emitting a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between the levels. E.g. transitions to n = 1 give the UV (Lyman) series, to n = 2 the visible (Balmer) series, to n = 3 the infrared series.

• Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels; light is emitted when the electrons fall back to lower energy levels.
• The energy differences between levels are different for Ca and Na, so the photons emitted have different frequencies/wavelengths (ΔE = hf), giving different colours.

Sketch: log IE rises steadily from IE1 to IE6 (general increase), with one large jump only between IE2 and IE3.

Why: Ca is [Ar]4s2; the first two electrons come from the 4s shell, the third from the inner 3p sub-level, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded.

(i) Four horizontal lines labelled n = 1 to 4, getting closer together at higher energy (converging).

(ii) Downward arrows from n = 3 → n = 2 and n = 4 → n = 2 (Balmer/visible series).

(iii) E = hf = 6.63 × 10−34 J s × 3.28 × 1015 s−1 = 2.17 × 10−18 J (per atom). The convergence limit corresponds to removing the electron from n = 1 to n = ∞.

(iv) λ = c/f = 3.00 × 108 ÷ 3.28 × 1015 = 9.15 × 10−8 m

(i) 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p5 or [Ar] 4s2 3d10 4p5.

(ii) Valence shell: one 4s box (lower energy) with a paired ↑↓, and three 4p boxes (higher) containing ↑↓, ↑↓, ↑ (Hund’s rule – pair only after each box has one).

Sketch: IE1 < IE2 < IE3 < IE4 < IE5 (always increasing), with the largest jump between the 3rd and 4th ionization energies.

Why: boron (1s22s22p1) has 3 valence electrons; the 4th electron is removed from the inner 1s shell, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded.

Four increasing points with a large jump between IE1 and IE2, then smaller increases from IE2 to IE3 to IE4. Why: Na has one outer (3s) electron; the 2nd electron comes from the full inner 2p sublevel, closer to the nucleus.
1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6 – the 4s electrons are lost first. Full configuration needed, not [Ar].

N vs C: N has a greater nuclear charge (one more proton) with electrons in the same 2p sublevel, so its electrons are held more strongly.

N vs O: O has one doubly filled 2p orbital; repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove. N has only singly occupied 2p orbitals (2p3, half-filled).

The bond in O2 (double bond) is stronger than the bonds in O3 (bond order 1.5), so O2 needs higher-energy (shorter-wavelength) UV to break it.

Ozone absorbs lower-frequency/longer-wavelength UV that O2 cannot, so together they absorb a wider range of harmful UV and less reaches the Earth's surface.

(i) Steps 1 and 3 (bond-breaking steps, which absorb UV).

(ii) Energy per O2 molecule: E = 498 000 J mol−1 ÷ 6.02 × 1023 mol−1 = 8.27 × 10−19 J.
λ = hc/E = (6.63 × 10−34 × 3.00 × 108) ÷ 8.27 × 10−19 = 2.40 × 10−7 m.
(Alternatively for ozone, using a bond enthalpy between 200 and 400 kJ mol−1, e.g. 300 kJ mol−1 → λ ≈ 3.99 × 10−7 m.)

p2.key:
(i) Any two, e.g.: it applies only to one-electron species (H); it does not show sublevels/orbitals (s, p, d); it treats electrons as particles in fixed orbits rather than as waves/probability clouds; it cannot explain the relative intensities of lines or fine structure.

(ii) X: upward arrow from n = 1 to n = ∞.

(iii) Z: arrow from n = 3 down to n = 2 (red line of the Balmer series, 656 nm) — the smallest energy gap that ends at n = 2.

(i) Fe2+: 1s22s22p63s23p63d6 (4s electrons lost first).

(ii) Fe is [Ar]3d64s2: the first 8 electrons come from 4s and 3d. The 9th is removed from the 3p sublevel, which is lower in energy/closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it is much more strongly attracted — hence the large jump.
